idiom_name: static readonly field / static constructor / Lazy<T>
implementation_notes: C# initializes a type before its first static member access or instance creation, and a static constructor runs at most once under a per-type lock, so the runtime performs the first-use ordering for you: a static readonly field initialized at its declaration is the idiomatic replacement for both classic idioms (the docs prefer field initializers over an explicit static constructor because the presence of a static constructor suppresses the beforefieldinit relaxation). For genuinely deferred construction use System.Lazy<T>, thread-safe by default with LazyThreadSafetyMode.ExecutionAndPublication. Keep type initializers short and non-blocking: they run under that lock and are never retried after an exception.
pitfalls: If a static constructor or field initializer throws, the runtime never retries it: the type stays unusable for the life of the application domain and later accesses fail with TypeInitializationException (or the original exception) again and again.
A static field initializer that creates an instance of the same type runs before the static constructor - the documented singleton exception to the 'static constructor first' rule.
Static constructors execute while a per-type lock is held: blocking inside one (waiting on tasks, locks or Parallel.* operations) risks deadlocks and stalls every other thread touching the type.
Lazy<T> caches the exception thrown by its factory by default, so every later Value access rethrows; only LazyThreadSafetyMode.PublicationOnly re-runs the factory.
Without an explicit static constructor the runtime is free to run initializers earlier than first access (beforefieldinit), so 'on first use' is a permission, not a promise.
